[1;97m1.4 — what just happened[0m

When you type [92mwhoami[0m and press Enter:

  1. The terminal hands your line to [36mthe shell[0m.
  2. The shell looks for a program named [92mwhoami[0m.
  3. It runs it.
  4. The program prints to [36mstandard output[0m — your screen.
  5. The shell shows the prompt again, ready for the next command.

The shell is not "Unix." It is a program — a [36mcommand interpreter[0m.
The terminal is a window that lets you talk to the shell. The program
[92mwhoami[0m is a third thing — it runs, prints, and exits.

You will keep these three apart for the rest of this tutor:
  [36mterminal[0m  →  [36mshell[0m  →  [36mprogram[0m

[36mAbsolute paths[0m start from the root, with [95m/[0m:
  [90m/etc/hosts[0m
  [90m/usr/bin/vim[0m

[36m~[0m is short for your home folder. [90m~/notes[0m means
[90m$HOME/notes[0m.

[91mPredict before you act.[0m  If you're in [90m~/projects[0m
and you type [92mcat notes.txt[0m, the shell looks for
[90m~/projects/notes.txt[0m. If you mean a different folder, name it.

You speak to it, it answers back.

[1;97m4.1 — reading a command[0m

A shell command has a small grammar:

  [36mcommand  options  arguments[0m

Examples:
  [92mls[0m
  [92mls -l[0m                    [90m# one option, no argument[0m
  [92mls -l /etc[0m               [90m# option + argument[0m
  [92mwc -l poem.txt[0m           [90m# count lines in a file[0m
  [92mecho "hello world"[0m       [90m# argument with a space — quoted[0m

[91mSpaces matter.[0m  The shell splits on spaces. If a filename
has a space, [36mquote it[0m or the shell will see two arguments:

  [92mvim "my notes.txt"[0m       [90m# opens one file[0m
  [92mvim my notes.txt[0m         [90m# opens TWO files: 'my' and 'notes.txt'[0m

[36mcommand -v[0m asks the shell whether a command exists.
  [92mcommand -v ls[0m            [90m# prints the path; exits 0[0m
  [92mcommand -v vim[0m           [90m# does Vim exist on this system?[0m
  [92mcommand -v vimtutor[0m      [90m# does vimtutor?[0m

[1;97m4.2 — the pipe[0m

A [36mpipe[0m ( [92m|[0m ) sends the standard output of one
command into the standard input of the next. [91mMost important idea
in the shell.[0m

[92mwc[0m alone counts:
  [92mwc -l poem.txt[0m          [90m# lines in poem.txt[0m

[92mwc[0m via pipe counts [36mwhatever you piped in[0m:
  [92mseq 1 100 | wc -l[0m       [90m# 100[0m
  [92mls /usr/bin | wc -l[0m     [90m# how many programs are installed[0m

Pipes stack:
  [92mls /usr/bin | sort | head[0m        [90m# list → sort → first 10[0m
  [92mls /usr/bin | grep ^a[0m            [90m# names starting with 'a'[0m
  [92mls /usr/bin | grep ^a | wc -l[0m    [90m# …and count them[0m

Things to notice while you try these:
  - [92m|[0m is Shift+Backslash on most keyboards.
  - Each piece is a normal command; only the connector is new.
  - The pipeline runs left-to-right; output flows.

This is the most important idea in this stage.

When you open a file in Vim, Vim [36mreads it into a buffer[0m —
a copy in memory. Your keystrokes change the [36mbuffer[0m, not
the file. The file on disk only changes when you [36mwrite[0m the
buffer back.

       (read)                  (edit)                     (write)

That's why Vim has separate commands for save and quit:

  [92m:w[0m    write the buffer to the file
  [92m:q[0m    quit (only if there are no unsaved changes)
  [92m:q![0m   quit and discard unsaved changes
  [92m:wq[0m   write, then quit
